name: Dimorphism theory

lead: Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framing that faces differ between the sexes in measurable ways, and that more strongly sex-typical features are more attractive: a pronounced jaw and brow and defined cheekbones in men, softer, more youthful features in women. Users apply it to choose beards, fat loss, haircuts and sometimes procedures that sharpen masculine features.

Proponents point to hormones, especially testosterone during puberty, shaping facial bone and soft tissue, with observers reading the features as signals of health. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness exists and is mixed: preferences for masculine male faces shift with factors such as menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, relationship status and country, and some studies find little link once perceived health is accounted for.

paras: People use it as a checklist for what to emphasize: lower body fat to show jaw and cheekbones, a beard to add jaw definition, and hairstyles that frame the brow. Some look into hormonal or surgical routes, which are covered in separate entries.
The theory itself is a descriptive framework with no direct risk. Hormone use or surgery to change facial structure carry their own medical risks.

angle.text: Forum users treat masculine features such as a strong jaw and defined cheekbones as central to male attractiveness, and use the idea to choose beards, fat loss or procedures that emphasize them. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness is real but mixed.

lead: Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framework that treats how masculine or feminine a face and body look as a main driver of attractiveness. Members use it as a checklist for improvement: a strong jaw, defined brow and broad frame for men, and softer, more youthful features for women, with grooming, body composition, hair, facial hair and sometimes procedures chosen to push features toward the sex-typical end.[1][2]

The idea overlaps with an academic literature on facial sexual dimorphism. A widely cited review of the evolutionary psychology of facial beauty argued that averageness, symmetry and sexual dimorphism are good candidates for biologically based standards of attractiveness, with meta-analyses indicating that all three are attractive in male and female faces across cultures.[3] Other work reports that preferences for masculine male faces vary with factors such as menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, relationship context and country.[4]

Because the term is a community framework rather than a single formal theory, forum discussion ranges from simple observations about height and jaw width to measurement schemes, such as a lower-face-to-skull-height ratio, and to questions about whether testosterone changes the face.[5][6][7]
infobox: More sex-typical facial features are rated as more attractive

paras: In forum discussion the term describes how masculine or feminine a face appears, with features such as jaw width, brow ridge, cheekbone prominence and facial hair on one side and softer, more youthful proportions on the other. Members use it to explain ratings and to decide which features to improve.[8]

Outside the community the subject is studied as sexual dimorphism and facial masculinity or femininity. In humans, males on average are taller and heavier than females and have denser bones, with testosterone levels roughly ten to twenty times higher in adult males.[8] Hair distribution, skin thickness and colour, and body proportions also differ on average.[8]

A looksmax.org thread on the topic argues that dimorphism underlies much of why looks seem subjective, pointing to height pairing, skin tone and youthfulness as traits that differ by sex and shape partner preferences; replies in the same thread dispute which traits count as masculine, feminine or simply robust or neotenous.[1]

Another thread reposts a measurement attributed to a facial-analysis site: the distance from chin to eyeline divided by chin to top of skull, described as a way to quantify lower-face height, with a taller lower third described as a masculine trait and a stated male range of about 50 to 53 percent.[2] Posters in that thread asked how the ranges are defined, illustrating that these metrics are community conventions.[2]
A further forum thread asks how far craniofacial development, and facial dimorphism in particular, can still change at the end of the teen years.[7]

Research on how observers respond to facial masculinity is mixed. One strand reports that women in the high-estrogen follicular phase were more likely to choose masculine faces than women who were menstruating or using hormonal contraception, interpreted under the so-called sexy son hypothesis.[4] Another reports that women who rate themselves as more attractive tend to prefer more masculine faces.[4]

Other work cited in the same review found no association between male facial masculinity and attractiveness among female judges, even while more feminine female faces were rated as more attractive, and one study argued that once perceived health is removed, masculinity makes little difference to male attractiveness.[4] A survey of heterosexual men in 28 countries found a preference for feminised female faces, stronger where national health indices were higher.[4]

The Annual Review of Psychology paper by Rhodes takes a broader view, concluding from meta-analyses that sexual dimorphism is attractive in both sexes across cultures, and discussing whether such preferences are adaptations for mate choice or by-products of how brains process faces.[3]

T Nation hosts a forum thread titled around whether testosterone replacement builds more masculine facial features, quoting an article in which a writer reports noticing more pronounced facial changes alongside muscle gain after starting treatment.[6] Hormone use carries its own medical considerations and is covered in separate entries.

No studies found on dimorphism theory as a looksmaxxing framework or on interventions designed on its basis. Related laboratory and survey research on facial masculinity, femininity and perceived attractiveness exists and is summarised above.[4][3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org dimorphism is treated as a central axis for judging faces and for choosing improvements, and is discussed alongside ratios and symmetry.[1][2]
